turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Margaret, come on through. Sorry about the wait this arvo. What's been going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, don't you worry about that. I was telling Lisa the jacarandas are nearly finished, gorgeous even on the footpath. She dragged me in, so here we are.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Thanks for squeezing us in. Her ankles have been puffing up, and the Webster pack's got a bit muddled, so I wanted you to go through the tablets.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Righto. Margaret, tell me about the ankles, in your own words.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, they're a bit chubby by tea time, both of them. The shoes won't go on properly. Not sore, just tight and puffy. Been like that a couple of weeks, I'd say.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yeah, two weeks. If I press the skin it leaves a dent.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your breathing? Any puffing?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, yeah. Just to the letterbox and back. Not every single time, but most mornings if I hurry. When it started, though, I couldn't tell you.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have a go for me. Weeks? Months?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, since Diwali or after, though we don't even do Diwali, that was next door. Um, last winter, or the one before. I honestly can't put a date on it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's alright, we'll leave the date. Any chest pain with the puffing?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. Heart's fine that way.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough? Fevers?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough, and I haven't had a temperature.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you wake up gasping at night, or need extra pillows?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I sleep flat, same two pillows I've always used. The neighbour's dog kicks off about five, so I'm awake, but that's not my lungs.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. What about the waterworks, any change?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I go a bit more after the water tablet, that's the point of it. No stinging or anything like that.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Never had a problem with tablets.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me what you're taking, even if you only know them by colour.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): There's the water tablet, and the frusemide, and the little white one, and the blood pressure tablet. Oh, and I used to have the cholesterol one. That's five, isn't it, or four. Lisa does the box.

[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mum, the water tablet is the frusemide, you're counting it twice. It's the one yellow tablet, 40 milligrams, every morning. The little white one is aspirin, 100 milligrams, with breakfast. The blood pressure one is perindopril, 4 milligrams, at night.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it really? I always thought the water one and the frusemide were two different things. The chemist said water tablet and I added one in my head.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Easy mix-up. And the cholesterol tablet?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The heart doctor stopped that. Dr Nguyen, at the clinic. My legs were aching something awful on it.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you remember the name, or the dose?
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Atorvastatin, 40 milligrams. He told her to stop, and she hasn't had it since.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was that, roughly?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Couldn't tell you. Ages ago. Not this year, or maybe it was. I don't know.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was before I moved in, so more than a year, but I haven't got the letter on me.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): And those muscle aches, are they still about?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No, they went once I stopped it. Legs are fine that way. Apart from the puffiness, obviously.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the heart failure, and the high blood pressure, they're still the ones on your file?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Blood pressure for years and years, and the heart failure they told me about after that stay in hospital. I've still got both.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): They're on the list. When you hurry and get puffed, is there any other feeling in the chest? You said there wasn't pain.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, if I rush there's a tight band across here, like someone's squeezing. Not a sharp pain. It eases if I stop and lean on the fence. I didn't think that counted as pain.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): It counts. I'm glad you said. How often does that happen?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Only if I hurry. If I dawdle I'm alright. Maybe three or four times a week.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pop up on the bed for me. Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 76 and regular, and your oxygen is 96 percent.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 152 a shocker? I had a scone at the markets on the way, and those navy shoes I bought there are a total write-off.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not shocking, no. Lungs are clear, no crackles, and the heart sounds are normal. There's pitting oedema at both ankles, up to the mid-shin.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): So the shoes weren't just me being vain.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I reckon the puffiness and the short wind are fluid building up on top of the heart failure. That tight band when you hurry, I won't call it angina for certain, but I can't rule it out today.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): So what are we actually changing in the box?

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd like to change the frusemide. Keep the 40 milligrams in the morning and add another 40 milligrams at lunchtime, so twice a day. Aspirin and perindopril stay as they are. Don't restart the atorvastatin.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Lunchtime as well? I'll live in the loo. Still, if the shoes go on, I won't argue.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): It should ease the swelling. I'll send you for a blood test in the next few days, kidney function and electrolytes, seeing as we're upping the water tablet.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can take her to the pathology at the chemist tomorrow morning.

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tea's fine, by the way, if you were about to ask. Legs up when you're sitting, go easy on the salt, and come back and see me in two weeks. Bring the Webster pack next time so we can check the lunchtime tablet is in there.

Patient reported sleeping flat with the same two pillows she has always used.
Doctor documented lungs are clear, in addition to no crackles.
Doctor advised the blood tests should be done in the next few days; caregiver said she could take the patient to pathology tomorrow morning.
Doctor specifically said tea is fine.
